spans.s:
stobha
(‘[letters used] in praise’)
------------------------------------------
In Sāmavedic chants, certain letters like hā-u, hā-i, hum, ho, ohā, ī and ū are used for musical interjections and interpolated into a सामन्. They are actually additional letters, not part of the letters of the original Ṛgvedic mantras which have been set to the musical notes of the Sāmaveda.
See also SĀMAVEDA.

stotra
(‘chant of praise’)
------------------------------------------
The word स्तोत्र is used in two senses: the Vedic and the paurāṇic.
The Vedic स्तोत्र is composed of verses taken mainly from the Ṛgveda. These verses are chanted as per the rules of intonation, especially those of the Sāmaveda.
A स्तोत्र always precedes a शस्त्र, (which is a laud that is just recited).
It may be in any one of the innumerable melodies (sāman), and stobhas (See STOBHA.) are added at appropriate places.
All stotras are chanted (or sung) by the उद्गातृ and his assistants, प्रस्तोतृ and pratihartṛ.
In Somayāgas the stotras are spread over all the three savanas. (See SAVANAS.)
According to the पुराणस् and devotional literature, a स्तोत्र is a hymn of the outpourings of the heart of a devotee of God. Stava, stuti and nati are the equivalents for the word स्तोत्र.
Though they may be in any language, either in prose or in poetry, only the Sanskrit hymnal literature will be considered here. They are legion.
The subject matter of these stotras may be ranging from the sublime heights of philosophy or mystical experiences, right up to petitioning for the small comforts of life here and now.
A few of these may be mentioned here: description of the form of God (or a deity) seen in a vision; request for pardon of sins committed knowingly or unknowingly; prayer for the removal of problems and difficulties and request for the grant of the good things of life; desire for obtaining devotion, knowledge and detachment that help one in spiritual life; a spontaneous outburst of emotion after deep spiritual experience and so on.
Stotras containing 108 names, 300 names or 1008 names of a deity are also commonly met with. They are used mostly in ritual chanting or ceremonial worship.
Another type called Suprabhāta-stotras (‘good-morning hymns!’) are also quite common and popular. Hindu tradition prescribes that these stotras can be chanted after meditation or worship.

stoma
(‘praise’)
------------------------------------------
Stotras are Ṛgvedic mantras set to the Sāmavedic tunes.
A स्तोम is a group of such verses and has several names depending on the number of repetitions. They are, for instance, pañcadaśastoma (15), saptadaśa-स्तोम (17), ekaviṁśastoma (21) and so on.
These stomas are arranged in two or more different varieties called viṣṭuti.
For instance, the ājyastotra (chanted during the morning pressing of सोम juice), consists of three verses (Ṛgveda 6.16.10-12) which can be called a, b and c. Then in a pañcadaśastoma of 15 verses the arrangement will be as follows:
1st paryāya or round—a a a b c;
2nd paryāya or round—a b b b c;
3rd paryāya or round—a b c c c.
This is called pañcapañcinī-viṣṭuti.
